blocks.text: A man with slowly worsening stiffness cannot start walking and freezes at a doorway, yet when a strip of tape is laid across the floor he steps over it smoothly. His muscles, spinal cord and motor cortex are intact. What is faulty is the deep circuit that decides which movement to release and which to hold back.

blocks.markdown:
The **basal ganglia** are a group of deep grey-matter nuclei that **select and scale voluntary movement** by modulating thalamic input to the cortex. They do not project directly to the spinal cord. The main components are:

- The **striatum**: the **caudate nucleus** and the **putamen**, the input stage, separated by the internal capsule but continuous ventrally.
- The **globus pallidus**, with an **external segment (GPe)** and an **internal segment (GPi)**. The putamen and globus pallidus together form the **lentiform nucleus**.
- The **subthalamic nucleus (STN)** of the diencephalon.
- The **substantia nigra** of the midbrain, with the **pars compacta (SNc)**, dopaminergic, and the **pars reticulata (SNr)**, functionally similar to GPi.

The GPi and SNr are the **output nuclei**. They send tonic inhibitory **GABAergic** signals to the **thalamus** (ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei), which in turn excites the motor cortex. The STN is the main **glutamatergic (excitatory)** nucleus; most other basal ganglia neurones are GABAergic.

blocks.title: Disinhibition
blocks.text: Because the output nuclei (GPi/SNr) tonically inhibit the thalamus, movement is released by inhibiting the inhibitor. Reducing GPi activity removes the brake on the thalamus (disinhibition), so thalamocortical drive rises. Increasing GPi activity strengthens the brake.

blocks.markdown:
**Two pathways through the striatum.** The cortex sends glutamatergic input to the striatum. Striatal output (medium spiny neurones, GABAergic) takes two routes.

**Direct pathway** (facilitates movement): cortex excites striatal neurones expressing **D1 receptors**; these inhibit **GPi/SNr**; the thalamus is disinhibited; thalamocortical excitation increases.

**Indirect pathway** (suppresses competing or unwanted movement): cortex excites striatal neurones expressing **D2 receptors**; these inhibit the **GPe**; GPe normally inhibits the STN, so the **STN is disinhibited** and excites GPi/SNr; the output nuclei inhibit the thalamus more; thalamocortical drive falls.

**Dopamine** from the SNc **excites the direct pathway (D1)** and **inhibits the indirect pathway (D2)**. Both actions favour movement.

rows: Striatum to GPe, to STN, to GPi/SNr

blocks.title: Tracing the direct pathway
blocks.prompt: Show how cortical activation leads to more thalamocortical drive through the direct pathway, labelling each synapse as excitatory (+) or inhibitory (-).

steps.text: Cortex to striatum (D1 neurones): glutamate, so excitatory (+). Striatal activity rises.
Striatum to GPi/SNr: GABA, so inhibitory (-). GPi/SNr firing falls.
GPi/SNr to thalamus: GABA, so inhibitory (-). With less GPi firing, thalamic inhibition falls (disinhibition).
Thalamus to cortex: glutamate, so excitatory (+). Thalamocortical drive rises.

blocks.answer: Net sign: (+)(-)(-)(+) = excitatory overall. The direct pathway facilitates movement through two inhibitory steps in series (a double negative).

blocks.markdown:
**Parkinson disease (PD).** Degeneration of **SNc dopaminergic neurones** removes dopamine from the striatum. Loss of D1 excitation weakens the direct pathway, and loss of D2 inhibition strengthens the indirect pathway. Both effects **raise GPi/SNr output**, which **over-inhibits the thalamus** and reduces cortical drive. The clinical result is **hypokinesia**: bradykinesia, rigidity, a rest tremor and postural instability.

**Huntington disease (HD).** An autosomal dominant CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene on chromosome 4 causes degeneration of striatal medium spiny neurones, particularly those of the **indirect pathway**, early on. Loss of indirect pathway activity means less inhibition of the thalamus: thalamocortical drive is **excessive**, producing **chorea** (involuntary, irregular, flowing movements), with cognitive decline and psychiatric disturbance. The caudate shows marked atrophy.

blocks.title: Parkinsonian circuit change step by step
blocks.prompt: Explain how loss of nigral dopamine produces bradykinesia, using the two pathways.

steps.text: SNc neurones die, so striatal dopamine falls.
Direct pathway: D1 neurones lose their dopaminergic excitation, so GPi/SNr is less inhibited and fires more.
Indirect pathway: D2 neurones lose dopaminergic inhibition, so they inhibit GPe more, which disinhibits the STN; STN excites GPi/SNr further.
Both effects increase GPi/SNr firing, so thalamic inhibition increases and thalamocortical drive falls, giving bradykinesia.

blocks.answer: Reduced direct and increased indirect pathway activity both raise GPi/SNr output and suppress thalamocortical drive: hypokinesia.

rows: Increased GPi/SNr output; decreased thalamocortical drive
Loss of striatal GABAergic neurones (indirect first)
Decreased GPi output; increased thalamocortical drive
STN excitation of GPi lost; thalamus disinhibited

blocks.title: Hypokinetic versus hyperkinetic
blocks.text: Too much GPi/SNr output means too little movement (Parkinson disease). Too little GPi output means too much movement (Huntington chorea, hemiballismus). Work out the sign of each synapse rather than memorising the disease.

points: The basal ganglia comprise the caudate and putamen (striatum), the globus pallidus (GPe and GPi), the subthalamic nucleus and the substantia nigra (SNc and SNr).
The GPi/SNr tonically inhibit the thalamus; the direct pathway disinhibits it (facilitating movement) and the indirect pathway strengthens the inhibition.
Dopamine promotes movement by exciting D1 (direct) and inhibiting D2 (indirect) striatal neurones.
Parkinson disease raises GPi/SNr output (hypokinesia); Huntington disease and STN lesions lower it (hyperkinesia).

questions.stem: Which two nuclei together make up the striatum?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the striatum is the caudate plus the putamen.
distractorRationale.b: Putamen plus globus pallidus form the lentiform nucleus.
distractorRationale.c: These are separate components of the circuit.
distractorRationale.d: The thalamus is not part of the basal ganglia.

questions.explanation: The striatum is the input nucleus, consisting of the caudate and putamen. The putamen with the globus pallidus makes up the lentiform nucleus.

questions.stem: Which basal ganglia nucleus is the main source of glutamatergic (excitatory) projections within the circuit?

distractorRationale.b: Correct: the STN is the main excitatory nucleus of the basal ganglia.

questions.explanation: The subthalamic nucleus uses glutamate and excites the GPi and SNr. Most other basal ganglia neurones are GABAergic.

questions.stem: The lentiform nucleus consists of which structures?

distractorRationale.b: Correct: the lens-shaped lentiform nucleus is putamen plus globus pallidus.
distractorRationale.c: The caudate is not part of the lentiform nucleus.

questions.explanation: The putamen lies lateral to the globus pallidus and the two together form the lentiform nucleus. The caudate is separate and forms the striatum with the putamen.

questions.stem: Which description of the direct pathway is correct?

options.text: Striatum inhibits GPi/SNr, which disinhibits the thalamus and facilitates cortical activity
Striatum excites GPi/SNr, which inhibits the thalamus
Striatum inhibits GPe, which excites the thalamus directly
Cortex inhibits the striatum, which excites the thalamus

questions.correctOptionText: Striatum inhibits GPi/SNr, which disinhibits the thalamus and facilitates cortical activity

distractorRationale.a: Correct: inhibition of an inhibitory output nucleus releases the thalamus.
distractorRationale.b: Striatal output is inhibitory, not excitatory.
distractorRationale.c: That mixes the indirect pathway with a non-existent direct excitation of the thalamus.
distractorRationale.d: Cortical input to the striatum is excitatory.

questions.explanation: Striatal D1 neurones inhibit GPi/SNr. Since GPi/SNr normally inhibit the thalamus, less GPi output means less thalamic inhibition and more drive to the motor cortex.

questions.stem: Activation of the indirect pathway has which net effect on thalamocortical output?

options.text: Decreased, because STN excitation of GPi/SNr increases thalamic inhibition
Increased, because the STN inhibits GPi

questions.correctOptionText: Decreased, because STN excitation of GPi/SNr increases thalamic inhibition

distractorRationale.a: Striatal D2 neurones inhibit GPe, they do not activate it.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: GPe inhibition releases the STN, which excites GPi/SNr and inhibits the thalamus more.
distractorRationale.d: The STN is excitatory to GPi.

questions.explanation: In the indirect pathway striatal D2 neurones inhibit GPe, which disinhibits the STN. The STN excites GPi/SNr, strengthening inhibition of the thalamus and reducing cortical drive.

questions.stem: True or false: the output neurones of the globus pallidus internal segment are GABAergic and tonically active at rest.
questions.explanation: GPi neurones fire continuously and release GABA onto the thalamus, acting as a tonic brake. Movement is released when this brake is lifted by the direct pathway.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man treated with a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist (an antipsychotic) develops slowness and rigidity. Which circuit change best explains this drug-induced parkinsonism?

options.text: Blocking D2 receptors removes dopamine's inhibition of the indirect pathway, raising GPi output and reducing thalamocortical drive
Blocking D2 receptors destroys SNc neurones
Blocking D2 receptors activates the direct pathway
Blocking D2 receptors increases GABA release in the thalamus directly

questions.correctOptionText: Blocking D2 receptors removes dopamine's inhibition of the indirect pathway, raising GPi output and reducing thalamocortical drive

distractorRationale.a: Correct: functional dopamine deficiency at D2 receptors mimics Parkinson disease.
distractorRationale.b: The drug blocks receptors; it does not kill neurones.
distractorRationale.c: D1 receptors drive the direct pathway; D2 blockade does not activate it.
distractorRationale.d: The effect is through striatal D2 neurones, not direct thalamic GABA release.

questions.explanation: Dopamine normally inhibits striatal D2 neurones of the indirect pathway. Blocking D2 receptors releases that inhibition, increasing indirect pathway activity and GPi output, so movement is suppressed.

questions.stem: Early neuronal loss in Huntington disease predominantly affects which cells, and what is the consequence?

options.text: GABAergic striatal neurones of the indirect pathway, causing chorea

questions.correctOptionText: GABAergic striatal neurones of the indirect pathway, causing chorea

distractorRationale.b: Correct: loss of indirect pathway activity reduces inhibition of the thalamus and produces chorea.
distractorRationale.c: That describes lower motor neurone disease.

questions.explanation: Huntington disease selectively damages striatal GABAergic medium spiny neurones, with indirect pathway neurones affected early. Reduced indirect pathway activity means less thalamic inhibition and excessive involuntary movement.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old hypertensive man suddenly develops violent, flinging movements of his right arm and leg. Imaging shows a small infarct in the left subthalamic nucleus. Using the circuit, explain why this lesion produces excessive movement rather than weakness.
markingGuide: The STN is glutamatergic and excites GPi/SNr
Loss of STN drive reduces GPi/SNr output
The thalamus is disinhibited and thalamocortical drive increases
Result is a hyperkinetic disorder (hemiballismus) rather than paralysis
Contralateral (right-sided) limbs affected because the left basal ganglia act on the left motor cortex, which controls the right body
questions.explanation: Without STN excitation, GPi/SNr fire less and release the thalamus from inhibition, so cortical motor drive is excessive. Because the left cortex controls the right body, the flinging appears in the contralateral limbs.

questions.stem: Compare Parkinson disease and Huntington disease in terms of the neurones lost, the effect on GPi output and thalamocortical drive, and the type of movement disorder.
markingGuide: Parkinson disease: loss of SNc dopaminergic neurones
Reduced direct and increased indirect pathway activity raises GPi/SNr output
Thalamocortical drive falls: hypokinesia (bradykinesia, rigidity, rest tremor)
Huntington disease: loss of striatal GABAergic neurones, indirect pathway early
GPi/SNr output falls, thalamocortical drive rises: hyperkinesia (chorea)
Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant CAG repeat disorder
questions.explanation: The two diseases lie at opposite ends of the same circuit. Parkinson disease over-inhibits the thalamus and slows movement; Huntington disease under-inhibits it and produces chorea.
